utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Yes, your Honours, we have a new witness for today. For the information of your Honours, we have only two witnesses left for this week, because things went rather quickly, and we will have only two witnesses in The Hague for this week, the coming witness and the next one. The new witness we are going to call today is Zoran Ninkovic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can you invite him? (Witness enters court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please swear the witness. Mr. Zoran Ninkovic (sworn) Examined by Mr. Turone JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am Giuliano Turone, prosecuting attorney. I am here with my co-counsel, Ms. Teresa McHenry, and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten, case manager. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: May we have the appearances on the Defence, please? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. In the team with me is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence Attorney for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I am from Croatia, and in the team with me is my co-counsel Mr. Michael Greaves, the Defence Attorney from the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. My co-counsel is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, appearing here on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Ms. Cynthia McMurrey from the United States. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir. Would you please state your full name for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): My name is Zoran Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born 27th December 1959.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Serb by nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, what education did you receive? I mean, what kind of schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished the elementary school in Konjic and the secondary school in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your profession in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was auto mechanic and I worked for Konjictrans in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in Konjic in the months of April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May and April of 1992 I was on the territory of the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, did you remain in Konjic town in those two months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Donje Selo until May 15th and after May 15th I was in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say if there was any specific reason why you moved to Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The particular reason was that my mother-in-law lived up there, that is the mother of my wife lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say approximately the date when you moved to Bradina. Can you repeat that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left around May 15th, 1992 from Donje Selo. I left Donje Selo and on that same day I arrived in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bradina -- where did you live in Bradina? Which house did you live in in Bradina? Your mother-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived with my mother-in-law in Gornja Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, can you say on which day was the village of Bradina affected by military action or shellings, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shellings took place on 26th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night after the shelling? Did you move to a safer place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night between 26th and 27th May I spent in a hamlet called Barakusa where there was a house which was safer, because it had a very thick concrete slab on top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Barakusa part of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Barakusa is part -- it's a hamlet of some ten houses in Upper Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there spending the night in this house in Barakusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This house had two floors and there were about 100 persons there, including men, women, children and the elderly, all together on these two floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 100 people in the two floors of this house, is that correct, about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, did you personally know a man named Petko Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him? What kind of a relationship had you with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petko Gligorevic was my mother-in-law's first neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Petko Gligorevic also spend that night in that same house in Barakusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now did you personally know a man named Miroslav Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him from the street, from the restaurants, from the cafes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did Miroslav Vujicic also spend that night in the same house in Barakusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He spent the night there, together with his wife and his child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, sir, what happened to you the following morning, I mean the morning of May 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th May a group arrived in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A group of whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group of members of the Muslim army led by Mitke Pirkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were these people approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about ten of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some wore uniforms and maybe one or two did not wear them. They were armed but wore no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the ones who had a uniform, did you observe any insignia on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. I did not notice the insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What did these soldiers do when they arrived at this house in Barakusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ordered us all to come out of the house. They separated women and children and the men stayed there on this village road as they came out, and obviously I was there with them as I came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated by these soldiers on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were telling us that we were Cetniks, that we wanted to attack them, to kill them, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being arrested on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion we were not told anything about why we were being arrested. I guess because we were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Petko Gligorevic and Miroslav Vujicic arrested on the same occasion as you that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. , they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Ninkovic, do you personally know another man named Radoslav Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know him? Which relationship do you have with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since he worked in the garage of Sipad Konjic and I did the same kind of work at Konjictrans, we would visit each other. We would swap auto parts. He would come to my place of work and I would come over to his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Radoslav a relative of Miroslav Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radoslav is a brother of Miroslav Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Radoslav Vujicic also arrested in the same occasion, that same morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ninkovic, what happened to you after you were arrested in Barakusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought in front of Mico Kuljanin's restaurant and from there they escorted us on foot to beyond the tunnel, to the butcher Zelenovic. They took everything. They took everything. They made us take all the valuables out of our pockets. They said if they found anything with anyone they would kill them. That's where the mistreatment started. We were hit with the rifle butts, with some wooden sticks, and after some of this mistreatment we were put on a truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many prisoners were put on that truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 75 prisoners were put on this truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that they took your valuables on the occasion of your arrest. What did they take exactly from you? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I myself had some money, I had a wrist watch. They took my jacket off. I had to leave it behind. I was in an undershirt and pants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, did you ever get your property back later on or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. After being put in this truck together with other 75 people could you notice whether Petko Gligorevic and Miroslav Vujicic were also on the same truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was so tightly packed on this truck, the people were so tightly packed, that at that time I did not notice it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But anyway they were part of the 75 people who were arrested with you, you say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With this truck where were you brought right after getting into this truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we were put on the truck we were taken to the military facility of the former JNA in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately at what time did you arrive at Celebici that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 11 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was, you said, May 27th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 27th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ninkovic, just to get an overview and to give right away an idea to us, can you say immediately how long did you remain in Celebici in all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether with that day, that day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day from 11.00 in the morning, first dusk, 7.00, 7.30. When they took us to the hangar, it was growing dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question is another one. I wanted to get a general overview immediately and just give right away an idea to the Trial Chamber on how many days in all you spent in Celebici, and then we will go back to details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether I spent nine days in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Going back to the day of your arrival at Celebici, so 27th May, did the truck stop at the entrance of the camp or inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck came to a stop inside of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now tell us in detail what happened to you right after your arrival inside the camp in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the truck arrived in Celebici the canvass was rolled up and the gate was opened and on -- there were four or five soldiers on each side waiting for us and they had -- they beat us with some sticks and rifle butts, and we had -- we were made to come off the truck and line up against some concrete wall, which was a couple of metres high, and we were made to lean against -- put our hands up against the wall and we were -- the threat was made that we would be killed if we lowered our hands, and then the mistreatment started with blows with the rifle butts and with -- and groups would arrive and they would sort of beat each individual prisoner, and I was one among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you say in which position were these prisoners along the wall? Do you mean face to the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All prisoners were facing the wall, because it was ordered that nobody should turn around or put their hands down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were face to the wall together with the other ones. May I ask you whether there were more prisoners on your right or your left along this line along the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more prisoners to the right. On the left there were maybe about 10, 11 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe in some detail how was this beating carried on by these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers went from one prisoner to the next and they were sort of -- they determined how much they were going to beat each one, so that they beat up every individual prisoner, beat them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this collective beating last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This mass beating went on from 11.00 in the morning until 7.00, 7.30 in the evening, when it was growing dark and you couldn't see any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there several rounds of beating during this time between approximately noon and 7.00 pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I myself was only beaten once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the soldiers proceed in this beating and these hours of beating? Did they start from the end of the line, proceed along the line and then again in the other direction? I want some details about that and how that could take so many hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They started at the top to my right, and when they would finish they would come back to the top from my right and do it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the soldiers say anything while beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point a voice could be heard somewhere above us asking certain questions, which we answered in a chorus: "Yes, we will. Yes, we will". Finally the word -- the voice said: "Will you rape the boulas, the Muslim women?" So we answered: "Yes". The response was: "You will? Now you will see what will happen to you". Then they cursed us and started beating us again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason for answering "yes" on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was the fear that we felt, and I remember this particular question but I don't remember all of them. There were other questions that we had to answer with "yes". This particular question: "Will you rape the boula?", I didn't myself at first know what the word meant, so we all said: "Yes, we will". The soldiers then started all over again to beat the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say that there were different rounds of beating back and forth along the line, and approximately how long did every round of beating take, if you can say this approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally, when I was being beaten, I was hit twice with a wooden pole, a very heavy pole, but I couldn't say what it was. I think it was a wooden pole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive these two blows right at the beginning of this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when this first series of mistreatment started, that was when I was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which part of your body were you beaten on this first series?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One blow on my left shoulder and the other one on the right side of my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time during the beating when you could recognise any of the soldiers taking part in the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At one point when the soldiers appeared then some prisoners before me asked -- prisoners left of me asked if they could have some water. There was some water there. When he reached me, I asked and he said I could. Going towards the water I recognised Ramiz Cibo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Ramiz Cibo was employed as a supervisor in Konjictrans, the same company I worked in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the man who allowed you to go to drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the drinking water on your right or on your left? I mean, in which direction did you move in order to go to drink water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the left, left from the place where I stood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this drinking water far away on the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was just at the end of the line left of the column of prisoners. As the prisoners were standing, left of them, at the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you moved to the left in order to go to drink, could you see anything particular concerning any of the prisoners on your left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my left among those 10 or 11 people there was a man lying on the concrete. He was not standing; he was lying. I saw him with my own eyes lying on the concrete. He wasn't standing; he was lying down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we entered the hangar, we learned it was Petko Gligorevic, because just when we were entering the hangar, two of his brothers, Nenad and Predo Gligorevic were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from you was Petko Gligorevic in the line on your left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly number -- he was the fifth or sixth man to my left, because we were so fearful that it was impossible to count exactly how many people there were. We were so terrified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say very approximately at what time of the day did that happen, when you first saw Petko Gligorevic on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was somewhere in the afternoon, maybe an hour or two, because when one is standing against the wall with arms raised, one is terrified. You daren't look left or right. You have to look in front of you. So it's difficult to tell exactly, but I think it was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you brought back to the same position in the line after drinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was brought back to the same place where I stood before I went to drink water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see again Petko Gligorevic on the ground when you went back to your position after drinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him when I was going to have a drink and when I came back, when Ramiz was bringing me back to the same position where I stood before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Petko Gligorevic in the same position as you saw him while going to drink water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the same position. The man was lying on the ground, on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, during the time you moved towards the drinking water on your left and coming back to your position, could you notice whether Miroslav Vujicic was possibly one of the other prisoners on your left or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He wasn't on my left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you anyway notice at that time, going or coming back from the water, the position of Miroslav Vujicic anywhere along the line of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, did you have -- did you ever have any occasion to see Miroslav Vujicic again any time after your arrival at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally remember which was the last time you personally saw Miroslav Vujicic alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Miroslav Vujicic in the night between 26th and 27th in the cellar of the house in Barakusa with his wife and child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, Mr. Ninkovic, again when you moved to the drinking water on your left and when you came back to your position at the wall, did you recognise any other soldier or guard being present in the area of the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Coming back after having had some water, in my field of vision I saw Hazim Delic, who was on crutches. He had one of his legs in plaster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delic doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say where was he exactly? I mean, with respect to the line of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was behind the line of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what distance from the line of prisoners approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately some 15 metres from the back. Between the backs of the prisoners and himself there was about 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Delic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him also from the street by sight and going to Sipad Prenj, where he worked as a locksmith in the garage of the company Sipad Prenj. So going there I would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ninkovic, going back to this collective beating at the wall, were you personally beaten again after you were allowed to go to drink or in any of the following series of beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was coming back after drinking water, I asked Ramiz Cibo, as I knew him well, I asked him: "What are you doing?", but he had two men accompanying him whom I didn't know, and one of them hit me with a rifle butt and told me to go back to my place against the wall and to lift up my arms as high as I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that did you receive any more beatings or not -- at the wall, I mean, facing -- standing at the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. After you went back from drinking water to your position against the wall, did anything particular happen; I mean during the following series of beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right the beatings continued. I concluded that they must have selected some people and beaten them more. At one point a voice could be heard saying: "I can't stand this any more. Don't beat me any more", and then a couple of seconds after these words a shot was heard. I was so afraid that at that moment I didn't know what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had a shot on your right-hand side. Can you say approximately how far from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shot could be heard to my right. It was close because I could hear the shot very loudly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ninkovic, you said that this collective beating finished at about 7 o'clock pm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere between 7.00 and 7.30. It was May, it was getting dark, so when they stopped and when they led us towards the hangar, it must have been around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying you were led towards the hangar. Which kind of a hangar? Where were you brought then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were lined up in a column two by two and we were taken to the hangar, a large iron structure like a vast garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that hangar have a number or not? Do you know the number of this hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number was the so-called Number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you left the wall in order to reach Hangar 6, did you have a chance to see again Petko Gligorevic lying on the ground or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean the body of Petko Gligorevic had been removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, you didn't see it any more. Did you have any other chance to see Petko Gligorevic after that or his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you reached Hangar 6, was the hangar empty or were there already other prisoners inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangar was empty. We were the first to enter the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you sit inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sat, when you entered the door, the left end of the building, left of the iron door, because the door stretched across the whole front of the hangar. So I sat on the left-hand side of the wall, somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say who was sitting close to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Baco Kuljanin; then Nedeljko Samoukovic; Dragan Djordjic; Kuljanin nicknamed Futa; Stevan Gligorevic. They were mostly Gligorevics. These were the four or five people to my left and to my right when we were sitting in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Radoslav Vujicic inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That same evening after we had entered the hangar I saw Radoslav Vujicic, who was walking and crying, and who kept repeating: "What have they done? They killed my brother".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Radoslav Vujicic sitting inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He sat to my right inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was he also one of the persons close to you, sitting near you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the same row as me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say in more detail what did Radoslav Vujicic say about the killing of his brother, Miroslav?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That first night after entering the hangar he kept crying non-stop and saying: "Look what they did to me. They killed my brother", and he kept repeating the same sentence. He was crying. He was absolutely distraught, and he kept repeating this same sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he or any of the prisoners you mentioned sitting near you say anything more about the circumstances of the death of Miroslav Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were sitting next to me, no-one knew anything more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Radoslav Vujicic or any of the prisoners sitting with you say anything about the shot you heard while being on line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody said they heard the shot and everyone concluded that that was how Miroslav Gligorevic had been killed, because he wasn't there amongst us and his brother Radoslav kept repeating these words practically all night. They did this terrible thing to me. They killed my brother".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record I think you said Miroslav Gligorevic. You meant Miroslav Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miroslav Vujicic. Miroslav Vujicic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Ninkovic, do you have any knowledge of any other prisoner who lost his life after the beating you have been describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the beating a man whose name I don't know, an elderly man, who was brought to the hangar by one of the prisoners, he was there for about three days with us in the hangar, and after three days the guards came. A man in a white coat -- I concluded it must have been a doctor; I didn't know him -- and then the soldiers took out the body of this man. I really don't know what the man's name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So approximately how long did this old man, this body, remain in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was there for about three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this man put on a particular place inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was placed in the direction of the door, on the same side where the door was, and he was at the end of the line sitting against the wall. There was one wall and the other wall and the steel doors that stretched along the length of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe this body with some attention and can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any time whether this body, this man, had any movement or was motionless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man, when he was brought in, he was taken out of a wheelbarrow and placed on the floor, and he never moved. If I had seen him get up and sit down or something ... I didn't. He was lying down all the time, motionless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you hear him moaning or emitting any noise, any sound or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Thursday one could hear him. That was on the 28th, the morning. He was brought in in the night between 27th and 28th. On the 28th you could hear his moans. After that I couldn't hear him any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Going back now to the first moment you entered Hangar 6 and were sitting there with the prisoners you mentioned a while ago, did any of these prisoners sitting together with you say anything about the fate of Petko Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two brothers of his, Vojo and Petko Gligorevic. They were sitting against the left wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Petko Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Predo. Predo. Predo Gligorevic and the two brothers said that they had no brother any more, that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ninkovic. Did the number -- you said you arrived in a hangar which was empty and you were approximately 75 people. So did the number of prisoners in Hangar 6 have any variation after that period, the first period of time -- I mean during your stay there, I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The number increased. They were bringing in more prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain in much detail when did that happen and how many people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One evening when Radoslav Vujicic was beaten up somebody called him out from the door. It was night-time. Radoslav Vujicic was beaten up. After the beating, which lasted some 20 minutes, he was thrown back into the hangar like a sack. He was calling out and begging for help to reach the wall, because he couldn't move on his own. Then we could hear at the same time blunt blows outside and moans, because somebody else was being beaten up. So then I and Baco Kuljanin got up and we managed to drag Radoslav Vujicic next to us, because he was in such a bad condition that wherever we touched him, he would cry out: "Don't touch me. Don't touch me", so that we only just managed to pull him to the wall. At that moment somebody else was thrown in and we didn't know who it was at that time. Afterwards another six or seven prisoners were thrown in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mention any names of these five or six new guests of Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning when it had dawned we saw that Mirko Dordic had come, Mrkajic Mrki, known as Mrki, a football player, Kisa Kuljanin, Zuza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever interrogated by military investigators while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was called out once and Zovko Kuhar and Subasic interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say very approximately when did that happen during the period of time you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After about six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After, yes. Where in the camp did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had that command building there and we were taken down the road from the hangar, five of us. That's how they separated us, in fives, and we were taken there. Outside there was some kind of a table that was put outside. It was summer. This Zovko Kuhar and Subasic questioned me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember or do you know who called you out of the hangar in order to take you to the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A guard called me out, Kravar. His last name is Spago, first name Enid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Zovko Kuhar and another person were interrogating you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zovko Kuhar, the former investigator of the MUP, and Subasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this interrogation were you accused of anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically I was accused of being on the side of the Cetniks, that I was against the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign any record of statement, any piece of paper, after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did sign some small record, because I was not interrogated very much, maybe ten minutes in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the paper you signed or was that read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not read out to me. I was just given it and shown the place where to sign and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they ask you? Do you remember the specific questions they asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me why I went to Bradina, why did I leave the town, why didn't I stay in town, and whether I had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking a while ago about a mistreatment suffered by Radoslav Kuljanin -- I mean -- pardon -- Radoslav Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vujicic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same night, when five or six new prisoners came. Could you say do you know who called or took Radoslav Vujicic out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't. I don't know who did, because they were calling out from the other side of the door, and when they take the person out they close the door. From my vantage point it is impossible to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long could you hear blows and screams outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- could you see who was the person who returned Radoslav Vujicic into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was dark in the hangar. You couldn't see a metre in front of you when the door was closed. We couldn't see each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. So you said that you and another friend of yours helped Radoslav Vujicic to go back to his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded.)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe which kind of mistreatment of injuries he had at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He gave the answer to that. Every part of his body was hurting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already said that. Every part of his body was hurting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I want to ask him if he knows better and has to give us some specific description of any specific part of the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was night-time. It was night-time. Every part of his body was hurting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Carry on. I was just pointing it out. It was already on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about some specific injuries of Radoslav Vujicic coming back into the hangar that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night we couldn't see anything because it was dark. In the morning, when the day broke, when you could see in the hangar, Radoslav Vujicic was in such a poor state that he couldn't move. His both arms -- we could see the white of the bone on the forearms, on both forearms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe any other mistreatment of any other prisoner during the days you were in Hangar 6 suffered by any other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That same night Zeljko Klimenta, called Keljo, was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he called out of the hangar too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not in the hangar with us. He had been brought in, I don't know from where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what could you observe personally of the mistreatment suffered by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him the same morning and he was in a poor condition. He relieved himself in his pants. He couldn't get up, so he just had urinated at the place where he was lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What role did you observe, if you observed anything, what role did you observe Delic having in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic had a role that whenever he would come into the hangar we would have to get up and salute him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequently did you see him inside Celebici Camp during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would come in every day to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say what to do -- to do what, I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would call out prisoners and on one occasion -- this was during the day, 1.00 or 2 o'clock -- he came in. He asked Radoslav Vujicic, he said. "Brother, who killed you?". There was some kind of wooden crate for weapons, for rifles. He gave Radoslav something to drink. I know that there was something that was in a vial. The second time he started calling out prisoners according to some order -- I don't know what order that was -- and they were taken out of the hangar. At that time I did not know where they were going. Another group of about 15, 16 prisoners left after that and I was in the third group. I was called out. I was approximately 7th or 8th to be called out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you are talking about the last day in Celebici. We'll talk about that later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded.)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you have any knowledge about -- of who was the Commander of the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not know who was the Commander. The first commander, who introduced himself as a commander, was Rale Musinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him on the 28th, the next day, the day after I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him on any other occasion besides on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him on that day when I was in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What about who was the Commander of the Celebici Camp in general? Do you know anything about any other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later found out that Commander Pavo was Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time on 6th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember -- can you describe this occasion on June 6th when you saw Mr. Mucic in the camp the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking about that moment before we were called out. I was in the third group and Delic was calling us out. We were coming out one by one through the door, and in front of the door there was a van. To the right was Pavo standing and on the other side was Buric, who was the driver. At that time we were climbing into the van one by one and that was the first time that I saw Pavo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he talk to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mucic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how come you knew Mucic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were very few people in Konjic who did not know Pavo Mucic, so I knew him. I knew him from the street, from the cafes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So you didn't see him any other time in the camp (sic) but that on June 6th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw him. I did see him on other occasions, about two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean in Celebici or where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in Celebici. I saw him in Celebici for the first time on June 6th, in Celebici, when I was transferred from Celebici to the Sports Hall in Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that the first time and the last time, or was there a second time you saw Mucic in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He has answered that question. He has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ninkovic, did you -- do you know who was Mr. Mucic's superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were talking about this occasion about June 6th. Was that the day when you left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness' microphone be turned back on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. That's done. So you were giving us the account of your transfer from Celebici to Musala. Can you give us a very detailed account of that after Delic called you out from the hangar and what happened with that van you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While being called out by Delic, we would come out. As our name and last name were called out, we would come out through the door. In front there was a van of Fiat make. The door was open. On the right-hand side was Pavo Mucic and on the left was the driver, whose last name was Buric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you enter the van?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Of course he did. Of course he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please go on in your account. What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we sat in. They closed the door to the van. We didn't know where we were going. I didn't know where I was going. When they opened up the door, I found myself at Musala, in front of the Sports Hall. Mucic got out, opened the door and we entered the Sports Hall, where we were put in locker rooms. There were rooms there, like locker rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic sitting in the front of this van during the drive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything before the drive or during the drive or right after arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything during the drive. The front and the back of this van had a partition. There was a glass partition, so we couldn't hear each other, and even if he was talking something we wouldn't be able to hear him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So when were you released from any kind of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released on 31st August from any kind of detention. In fact, I was released from Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive a release document on that day, August 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did receive a document saying that I was being released from detention. Some 30 -- 30 something prisoners were called out and ones were being assigned to go to Brdjani and the other group was going to go to another village, and when my turn came, and Mucic was there, I told him: "Mr. Pavo, I don't want to go to Donje Selo". There was part of Konjic called Varda. He took the piece of paper and said: "What street?" I said: "Maksim Kujundzic". He said: "Fuck Maksim Kujundzic. Go on foot", and I stayed there then. That was the last time I saw Pavo during my stay in camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the release document -- was the release document given to you by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic gave it to me and in his hand, in his own handwriting, he wrote down "Maksim Kujundzic".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was the address you gave him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask the assistance of the usher to show a document to the witness which might be marked for identification, I believe with number 159, please. We have copies for your Honours. Defence lawyers have already this document. (Handed). Can you see the document, Mr. Ninkovic? Can you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document you received by Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the document I received from Mr. Mucic and what it says here: "Maksim K, 28 Konjic". That is what he wrote down in his own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see that your year of birth here is indicated as 1955. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is an error, because I was born in 1959. There in the Red Cross registration card the birth date is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So, your Honours, I would tender this document for admission and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But one is not a translation of the other. It is a different format altogether. This is a different translation -- different document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The formats are different entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The document was probably cut badly, because there is also this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The date of birth is right on top. I'm not sure if the same document has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The upper part of the photocopy actually is wrong. Probably we should eliminate this first part, which is part of another document, which is the Red Cross document. The real document is this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is not a translation of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The translation is a translation of this one. Again I see there is the same mistake of the document of yesterday. There is "her" instead of "his". We will also correct this in a better translation, your Honours. So we tender this for admission, Exhibit 159, and that is the end of my examination-in-chief, your Honours. Thank you very much. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay. I don't think I need call for any cross-examination now, since we are breaking for 30 minutes. We will have our 30 minutes break. When we return, then we'll start cross-examination. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Will you please invite the witness? Is the Defence sure about its cross-examination pattern? Is there anything to cross-examine? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, the Defence of Zejnil Delalic has no questions to put to this witness. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, the Defence of Zdravko Mucic has no questions for the witness. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Hazim Delic has no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we have no questions, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I thought as much. They had a different impression. Where is the witness so that we will formally tell him he is discharged (Witness re-enters court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Kindly remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still testifying under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It seems there is no cross-examination for him and there is consequently no re-examination, except you need him for other things. You don't need him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let's have your next witness, if you have any. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have to ask for a recess because we are not yet ready with our next witness. We should respectfully ask your Honours to allow us to bring our next witness after the lunch break, because we are not yet ready for the next witness. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Is this a trick on you by the Defence or what? I think it makes life easier for everyone. So we will have to recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Tribunal will now adjourn until 2.30. (12.10 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen: are you now ready with your witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, we are ready. I will point out that this is a protected witness and so the courtroom needs to be set up. The witness is Mr. D. (Witness enters court) Witness D (sworn) Examined by Ms McHenry JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we have appearances please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, your Honour, I am Teresa McHenry and I am here with co-counsel, Mr. Giuliano Turone and our case manager, Miss Elles van Dusschoten. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Defence, please. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I'm Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor of law from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, Defence Counsel for Mr. Pavo Mucic. With me is my colleague Michael Greaves, lawyer from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. My co-counsel is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. I am John Ackerman. I am representing Mr. Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Miss Cynthia McMurrey from the United States. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. You may proceed with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, am I correct that you have requested protective measures such that your identity and your face not be revealed to the public or the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): It is correct that I asked for protective measures so that my identity should not be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that you will be known then here today as Mr. D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to show the witness a piece of paper and, sir, I ask you to look at that and tell -- confirm that this is, in fact, your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, do you understand that if you are asked something and you believe the answer to the question may tend to reveal your identity, you may request the judges to give your answer in private session? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you originally from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by nationality a Croat. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr.s McHenry, let the witness be more composed so that he wouldn't move about too much, not to get into the problems of being disclosed. Let's get the technical people and tell them to deface, to take off his picture.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Actually what I'm asking is that he doesn't move too much so that the facial distortion should be well done, because if he moves there's a risk of him being seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I see. Sir, do you understand that it's helpful if you -- you don't have to be as still as a statue, but if in general you don't move back and forth, especially forward and back very much. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Could the permanent defacement of his face be made so that as long as it's within that perimeter it won't affect it, because he is not moving out of that area. That's possible? All they need to do is to deface the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask that the witness' microphone be turned on and I'll advise your Honours that during my examination-in-chief I'm going to request that we go into private session on two separate occasions, and this is now the first occasion that I would be requesting that we go into private session to ask a few questions about his background. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Inform them to get into private session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now back in public session. Sir, can you tell us whether or not you returned to the Konjic area some time in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall the date, but I think it was at the end of May in 1992. The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina had already started and with my wife I decided to transfer her from Mostar to Konjic or, to be more precise, a part of Konjic known as Buturovic Polje, where I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicate that you believe it was towards the end of May. Do you know whether or not you returned to Konjic before or after the attack on Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Konjic the day the operation in Bradina ended. Actually that was the day I arrived in Ostrozac. That is 14 kms from Konjic and I stopped there to convey to an inhabitant of the place some greetings from some people in Mostar. It was the afternoon and some units or groups of soldiers were already coming from the area where the military operations were being conducted, that is the area of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, upon returning to Konjic, did you report to any kind of political or military authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to get out of Mostar I had to have a special written permit from the by then already formed Croatian Defence Council. Following the instructions that I received when I was given this permit, my task was to report to the Croatian Defence Council in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, may I confirm that the Croatian Defence Council is commonly known as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is the abbreviation HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly what happened when you report reported to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was also told in Mostar that I had to go back to Mostar, because I was a citizen of Mostar, which I did not deny, of course, but when I arrived in Konjic with this permit, I went to the HVO and I reported to them, and I then said that I had to go back to Mostar. However, if I am unable to get into Mostar because of the constant shelling of the only way in and out of Mostar, I would come back to Konjic again. That was normal. That is for people to be going back and forth several times. So that maybe the second or third day after that I went back in the direction of Mostar, but the road, the Mostar-Goranci road, was under constant artillery fire, so that I did not enter the city and I went back to Konjic. That is what I told the people in the HVO and I said if they felt that I could join in the defence ranks there, that I was ready to do that. There was a man there -- I think but I'm not sure that his name was Zovko or something like that -- who told me that if I stayed I would be welcome, and that I should report to Goran Lokas. I asked what was this man doing, this Goran Lokas, but I knew him, because while I was working in the police, he too was head of department. Actually at that time he was known as the secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, as it was called then, and I said that I had nothing against reporting to him, thinking that he was working in a body of the Internal Affairs Secretariat. But he added that he was now working in the Military Investigating Commission. I agreed, and the next day I went to Konjic, because in the meantime I had been staying at Buturovic Polje, which is a local community belonging to the municipality of Konjic, an area that I originated from, where I was actually born. The next day -- I can't remember the date exactly, but this was probably the end of day -- I went to the HVO to report to Goran Lokas. They told me that Mr. Goran Lokas had had a traffic accident -- was involved in a traffic accident the day before and that I should come on another day to report to Ivica Azinovic. This was somebody I did not know and I didn't enquire either what his post was, but the next day I was informed through my wife's sister who lives in Donje Selo, or she used to live in Donje Selo -- this is in the immediate vicinity of Konjic -- and she told me that Miroslav Stenek had come to see her looking for me and that I should report to the HVO. Of course, the next day I went to the HVO. They told me I should wait for Mr. Ivica Azinovic. About midday of that day Ivica Azinovic appeared. Actually at the very entrance to the HVO premises a security man told me: "Here is Mr. Ivica Azinovic". When I addressed him, as far as I can recall, without even entering his office, or maybe he was still exchanging a few words with someone else at the time -- I'm not sure -- he turned around and told me to follow him. I did and in the courtyard of the building a vehicle was waiting and a driver, who had actually driven him there. He told me to sit down and that is how we left, without telling me where we were going or what we were going to do. Sitting in the car, I asked him: "And where are we going now?", and he told me that we were going to see Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I went to secondary school with Zejnil Delalic. I wasn't aware that he was there at that time, but I didn't find anything wrong with going to see him. So that in the meantime from the HVO premises to the house owned by Mr. Zejnil Delalic it took us a couple of minutes to get there only. We entered a large room in his house. Of course, as I knew Mr. Delalic, there was no need for any introductions by Mr. Azinovic, but when we entered, he said that we had come. There were some other people there, with whom I shook hands, but who I did not know at the time. I think I didn't know any one of them then. I know that Mr. Delalic introduced me. He said: "This is ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness has spoken his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you will just -- may we go into private session for one minute, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay. Let's go into private session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to introducing you to the other people by name, did Mr. Delalic say anything about what your duties were going to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was not offered to sit down but I saw that they were busy with something. He said -- as far as I can recall now the contents of what he said: "This person will continue to work in the Military Investigative Commission in Celebici". I think that he even said -- I think that he even told what part of the job I was going to do there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that there were any details spelled out about this. Maybe I asked whether I was going to start doing this the next day or something like that, and he said that Goran Lokas was not around, that he had a car accident, and that it would be desirable if I started on that job the very next day. If I msy answer a question in private, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We want to get into private session

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please hold on and we’ll go into private session (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are in public session again. Sir, at this time what did you understand Mr. Delalic's position to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time my understanding was that Mr. Delalic was either in some kind of headquarters or some kind of commander who is supposed to give this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What happened after you were told by Mr. Delalic about what kind of work you would be doing? Did you, in fact, then start working at the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The very next day I went to Celebici and joined this group. Among them were Miro Stenek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am not going to ask you the names now. I will ask that later in private session. Can you just tell us now, sir, so that the judges will have an overview, can you tell me approximately when it was that you stopped working at Celebici camp and I'm not asking for any details about why you stopped. I just wonder if you can tell us approximately when it was you stopped working at Celebici Camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to say, without mentioning all the names -- what I wanted to say was that Stenek was there, who was already working there, who was part of that commission, so that with his assistance I received these materials and I started working on them. As far as your other question is concerned, I think it was about a month, maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without giving their names at this time, can you tell us how many members of the Commission there were who worked at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were seven members of the Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you were working at the camp how often did you go to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, I went there every day. The Military Investigative Commission worked every day from 0800 hours until 1800 hours or maybe until 17:00 hours. I don't know. Except for Saturdays and Sundays -- sorry. I think except for Sundays, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to the work that you just described briefly in private session, did you also interrogate some prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was not frequent, but I was present on several occasions to these questionings and I conducted them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you, sir, to indicate that you didn't interrogate as many prisoners as the other persons on the Commission, because you were also doing the other work that you've already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the month or slightly less that you estimate you worked there, are you able to estimate approximately how many prisoners you yourself interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I think that there were about ten, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I also understand you, sir, to indicate that at the time you first went to Celebici some statements had already been taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The statements had already been taken from a number of arrested persons, that is the persons who were brought to the camp. Those were mostly individuals arrested in the area of Donje Selo, Pokojiste and some other villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you started your work, how did you know what to do? Was there a time that someone instructed you as to how the Commission should work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, when I took over this part of the job, which I was told that I would be doing, as I knew how to do it from before, I started working on it, but very soon -- I think it could have been 1st June of 1992 -- with the Commission in the premises in which we worked we had a meeting with Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting was announced the day before and it was said it was going to take place, and it did take place at the premises of the building where we worked, and this particular room was used as a dining hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that the meeting with Mr. Delalic occurred in the dining room of the building where you worked in the camp in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the building where you worked -- did it have a name? How was the building referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall what it was referred to as.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe generally where this building was and what else was present in this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building was to the left of the main gate. As you came to the camp it would be to the left of the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe it would be helpful -- was this building used for administration, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably during the former JNA time it was used for administrative purposes, and in this case it was also used as the administrative building, because this Commission was housed there. The Commander of this camp had an office there. That is how I was told that this title was, the camp commander, Zdravko Mucic; his deputy Hazim Delic, and there were some other rooms there which I wasn't looking at. Maybe they belonged to the persons who were -- who discharged guard duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let's go back then to this meeting that Mr. Delalic had in the administrative building. Can you just please tell us were all the Commission members there and what occurred during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were all there. Maybe somebody was absent, but it seems to me that they were all there. I know Mr. Mucic, the camp commander, and the other members of the Commission. I don't know the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please tell us what happened during this meeting, what occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting didn't last long. I know that at the very beginning Mr. Delalic read out to us some kind of order, which arrived by fax, or maybe some other way. I don't know. He read out the title to whom this order was directed. As far as I recall, the order was directed to all commands and staffs except for the Cetnik ones. That was approximately what it sounded like. I know that he laughed a little bit when he read that. It sounded a bit funny. The text was fairly short, something about combat operations in the wider area and the expectations of some combat operations, something to do with the Cetnik attacks and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delalic indicate where this order came from, who had issued it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he -- that this telegram was signed by -- I don't know what rank he read this person, but it said Mate Sarlija, "Daidza".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time did you know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had heard that for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With the usher's assistance I would like to show you a document, sir. This document has previously been shown to Defence Counsel. (Handed.) Am I correct that this would be document 160?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I need to use my glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I ask that you look at what has been marked for identification purposes as Prosecution Exhibit 160, and I ask if you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this is the contents of this message that was read by Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, was there any other -- other than reading this order, what was discussed during this meeting with Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he came to what he actually came there for. It was about how we were to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we", do you mean how the Commission was supposed to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is about the Commission, because the goal -- the aim of this meeting was to -- the work of this Commission, and before this meeting we had received in the Commission a typed text, in fact, the categories according to which all these prisoners were to be distributed. At that time Mr. Delalic was explaining these categories to us. As far as I can recall, he said that he had worked out these categories so that these prisoners could be classified according to the documents that was available. I think that -- it seems to me that there were nine categories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In addition to explaining the categories to you, was anything else discussed? For instance, was there any discussion about release documents or do you remember anything else that was discussed about the work of the Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The discussion was about creating the materials for analysis to sum up all the incriminating facts and all the acts and that on the basis of that decisions on the status could be made of these prisoners, and, of course, the measures that were to be taken accordingly.
