I don't know what else was discussed, but mostly about these issues, that there were a lot of these prisoners, that a lot of these materials were brought from the field, that should the Commission find out that there are weapons hidden in the field that was left behind belonging to these prisoners, that the military police were alerted in a timely fashion so that they could go out there and recover them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I would ask to go into private session again, because I think the next few questions I may ask might tend to reveal the witness' identity? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay. Let's go to private session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we are now back in public session. Mr. D, can you tell us did you and the other members of the Commission wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Commission wore uniforms, but not always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the uniforms have insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No-one at the time among the Commission members had any insignia, as far as I can recall. I didn't have a uniform for a long time, not for a long time, maybe a couple of days, and I know that I took this uniform and signed for it from Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where the guards were from; in other words, what group or entity they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know who the guards belonged to. I never saw any insignia, at least passing through there I never saw any insignia on them, but, to be quite frank, I didn't really look. I noticed only one guard, that when speaking he had an Albanian accent. Then I asked someone: "How come an Albanian is here?" Somebody told me that he had served in the former JNA there and that he had stayed on. He had joined the forces that were placed in the position of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At this time can you just very briefly describe what defence forces there were in Konjic at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was the essential. There was the Territorial Defence, the TO, then the HVO. However, at first there was the Patriotic League, the HOS. I don't know. I would see this on the licence plates of vehicles. At that time people would write those plates out themselves and probably, seeing the TO and the HVO, then others would put "HOS". I even saw "MOS", probably the Muslim Armed Forces. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the HOS, what did you understand the HOS to stand for and who did you -- did you have any information about where the members of the HOS that were in Konjic, where they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw vehicles with this sign a couple of times. I saw some young men who all came from the territory of Konjic. They were all young men. I can't say. I don't know where they had come from, anywhere outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going back now to the Celebici camp, what did you understand concerning who the detainees were, and I'm not asking their names; I'm asking if you could tell us your understanding of how they came to be in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, when I got there, there were a lot of prisoners there already. I saw these lists brought to us in the Commission by Mr. Mucic and the members of the Commission talked to Mr. Mucic, or if Mucic wasn't there, then it was Delic, which people needed to be interviewed in the course of that day, and of whom statements should be taken. So that, looking at those lists -- I can't remember now whether there was one list; I think there were several lists, probably in the order in which they were brought in or maybe from where they were brought in. But they were not only military conscripts. There were civilians there too. I saw some women on the list. So I understood that this must be a prison where persons were being brought in who had been captured in the area of combat operations or in connection with those combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand whether or not it was people who had been captured because they were part of the combat operations, or did you understand that all men from that area were captured? Can you explain a little bit about what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one thing what I understood and another what the practice was. The practice was to bring in virtually all males from the area of combat operations, and not only men but women as well, but there were men who were brought in who were outside the area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned previously the categories. Can you please explain to us what you remember about the various categories and how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, a lot of time has gone by. I can't remember quite clearly the contents of all the categories, but I think that the first category were men who had participated in the combat operations under arms and if there are documents to prove that they were armed in those operations and that they had killed somebody in those operations, that was the worst category. The second category would be somewhat milder cases, again armed men, captured in the area of combat operations but for whom it had not been established that they had killed anyone, which doesn't mean to say that they indeed hadn't. A third category was again something like that but the difference I think was that they had given themselves up, because these others hadn't surrendered, according to the documentation at least, but that they were forced to surrender. Then came the other categories. They were milder and, to tell you the truth, it was difficult to differentiate because you didn't know how to classify them into the sixth, fifth, seventh, and I didn't really agree with those categories, but that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then, sir, please explain how the categorisation process worked. Who decided what category to put someone in and what was the impact of somebody being in a particular category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having read these things, and we would get together, the Commission would get together from time to time, and when I read the documents referring to a particular person then I would read out the indications for each of the categories and evaluate which category that person belonged to. That was the duty of each member of the Commission. When dealing with a case each one of us had this list with the categories indicated to put down on the file and each prisoner had a kind of file, where everything related to that prisoner was placed. Then on the file, on the outside, we would put "1st category", "2nd" or "3rd", and I think that we even made lists on the basis of those filed after they had been classified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, sir, what, if anything, did you understand was supposed to be the result, the import of someone being put in the first category versus the seventh category, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We understood this classification as meaning that somebody who was deciding on the release of those prisoners, and it was not up to us in the Commission to decide on that, to group those files and thus provide easier access to the documents and easier decision on release, so that in my view, and probably in the view of the others too -- at least that is what they said -- after the third or fourth category, if the persons were already in the camp and after they had been interrogated, they should have been released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you described these files that were created and then the categorisation. What happened with these documents in the files that were created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what happened when we left, but while we were there and when we said that the prisoners had been categorised, I know that Mr. Mucic, when he came for the lists, would say that the decision on who would be released would be taken by commander Zejnil. That's what he said, which is something we, of course, didn't interfere with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these -- during the time you were working there, were these documents or files -- were they ever taken out of the Celebici Camp after you finished with one, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see that, nor was I able to see, but we prepared them and grouped them together so that -- according to category, so that they could be carried out because, as I said, we made a list, for example, of the sixth group or the fourth group category and attached to the list would be the appropriate files, so that the person who was deciding could be able to give his approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the Commission members who were creating these files did you ever see anyone else in possession of these files?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see, nor was it -- were they accessible to anyone else except Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic. I don't know any others. Whether Mucic, or at least that was how he behaved in front of us, whether he took them to Mr. Delalic, Zejnil Delalic, I didn't see him do that, but if he said that the decision would be taken by Mr. Delalic, then he probably took them to him, but I cannot expressly assert that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us how frequently you would see Mr. Mucic in the camp when you were doing your work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know whether he was there all day, but while I was working there, I think I saw him every day, once or twice. I only know that on one occasion somebody -- I don't know who -- was looking for him and somebody said that he was busy in the field and that he had stayed behind to have a good sleep, and that he would come later, but I didn't notice his absence, that he was absent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned briefly that Mr. Mucic had an office. Did you yourself ever have occasion to go into his office and on any of these occasions was he ever present in the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered his office without knowing that it was his at the very beginning of my work there. I asked for the written documentation that had been brought in from the field and which the Commission needed to study and investigate further. Then they told me -- I think somebody was with me then -- that this was to be found in Mucic's office, and that was the room where we were working -- in relation to the room in which we were working, the third room from us. I think so, in a series -- in a row of rooms. So then I found some papers in a sack and Mr. Mucic was there too, and he told me: "Here you are. This is it". I would take the papers from there and we would examine the papers, see what we needed for our further work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how was it that prisoners were brought to the administration building for interrogation and who decided they should be interrogated; in other words, would the Commission members decide themselves and then go out and ask for certain prisoners, or how did that -- can you explain how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that we received the lists from Mr. Mucic and then the Commission would write out the names of people they needed to interview, indicating the names of the prisoners that needed to be brought in for an interview. This list would be given to Mr. Mucic or his deputy, Delic, and as far as I know it was mostly Delic who did this, and I think Mucic said something to that effect, that a list needed to be made of who we needed and we should give that list to Mr. Delic and he would proceed further. Since there were several Commission members, several prisoners would be brought in. I think about ten people at a time were being prepared, were ready for this interview. None of the commissions -- at least I didn't see them -- nor did I ever go any further than that building. I saw -- there was frequent shooting there in that camp and when we were working through the window, through the glass panes, one could see that part of the camp from where the prisoners were being brought, and on a couple of occasions I saw several people lined up against the concrete supporting wall. They were facing the wall with their hands raised against the wall. I saw Delic there. He always carried a rifle with him on the ready, so to speak. They would fire above the heads of those people bursts of fire. Everybody could see this. All the members of the Commission could see this. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will have a break now and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.30 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. I see you are standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to raise a matter before we continue, if I could have the indulgence of the court to do that? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. What is the matter about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has to do -- I think this witness has either little or nothing to do with regard to my client, but I have been listening and have become concerned with a matter which may be better taken up with the witness not here. I'll leave that to the discretion of your Honours, but I think it might be better for the witness to withdraw for a moment while I raise this issue. I'm doing it more in the nature of amicus curiae than as an advocate in this case. I think it's something that should be brought to the court's attention and the attention of the Prosecutor but I am concerned that it maybe ought not to be done in the presence of the witness. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can lead him into the witness room for a few minutes: (Witness withdraws from court).

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Conditionally it might be better if we are in closed session, private session. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, I think so. Private session. Inform the technicians (In closed session).
